utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I do apologise to my learned friend. Just very brief issue I would like to address the Trial Chamber with regard to yesterday's transcript, which I think it's quite important for the interest of the Defence in terms of procedural issues, if you permit me just to briefly address the Trial Chamber with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, yesterday, during the cross-examination of my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio, I objected to certain questions. Actually, it could be find under yesterday's transcript LiveNote version page 50, and accordingly, 51. My learned friend, after my objection on line 18, said, inter alia, that -- I will quote him: "Firstly, if Your Honours please, I believe that the task of objecting to any questions on my part lies with Mr. Lukic and not with Mr. Pantelic." And then you gave certain instructions with that regard. The position of the Defence of -- I'm speaking on behalf of all three teams, because we have discussed that issue -- is the following: Due to the nature of the case, which is a joinder by its nature, sometimes there are certain, I would say, various and different approaches to certain issue, and after 175 days of proceedings in this particular case, we are very well aware that during all these previous days we were entitled to object, no matter which witness is in the dock, and strictly limited to the scope of the indictment, of the charges, and also in accordance with the strategy of particular defence of one team, which in practice means that when my learned friend ask Mr. Tadic with regard to the political prisoners, my basis for objection was that since my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic, was also charged in count 1 of the indictment with the coercion, arrest, et cetera, that it might be of certain impact to the defence of my client. So I kindly ask for the instructions with that regard, if the situation in future will arise, I believe that each of Defence teams could object to certain line of questioning which is strictly related to his particular client and his particular defence. I believe that my understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that there has to be some order in the manner the proceedings are conducted, and the Trial Chamber is of the view that each accused person has got two counsel who are supposed to work together and assist each other during examination-in-chief, cross-examination, examination by other counsel, and re-examination, and the Trial Chamber believes that that is sufficient. However, the Trial Chamber is flexible. If there is any piece of evidence which is of particular concern to another accused, then, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, counsel may be allowed to ask questions or to object in this case, but it has to be with the leave of the Chamber, because there has to be some order. And also, when an accused is giving evidence, the Trial Chamber has to be very, very careful that his attention is not distracted, and the Trial Chamber believes that only his counsel has gone in details with his instructions and is much better able to object. So those points must be borne in mind so that we have some order, and also the attention of the accused person is not distracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, may I just raise one very brief matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- before I proceed? Last week some 92 bis statements were provided to the Prosecution of certain witnesses, and the Prosecution has not yet filed a response. May I seek an extension of time in which to file the response to those 92 bis witnesses, to the close of business on Thursday afternoon? This, unfortunately, has come about because of Prosecution involvement in the preparing for this particular cross-examination. I regret it, but I submit that it won't greatly affect the overall schedule of the trial or prejudice the rights of the Defence if you grant us an extension of time until Thursday close of business. And so may I orally make that application and seek permission to put in a response to those statements by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean Thursday, the 26th or the 27th of February? This week? MR. DI FAZIO: This week. This week. This Thursday, close of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 27th. Okay. Any objection from the Defence? I see none. The extension is granted. The motion is granted to extend the time within which the Prosecution may respond to statements taken under Rule 92 bis, and the time is extended up to Thursday this week, which is the 27th of February, by 1730 hours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination may proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, yesterday you said that as chief of civilian protection, you're responsible for the protection of cultural monuments. You agree, don't you, that the Catholic church -- sorry. I withdraw that. You agree, don't you, that of the three cultural -- sorry, religious monuments in Bosanski Samac, the orthodox church, the mosque, and the Roman Catholic church, two were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think we should be aware, of course, that in the fifth amended indictment, the reference to "religious and cultural institutions" was added in as an amendment in the fifth amended indictment. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We should also be aware in terms of your cross-examination that in the Trial Chamber's written reasons for motion - sorry - for decision on motions for acquittal, dated 11th October, 2002, that this Trial Chamber decided that in paragraph 6 on page 8, that the destruction or wilful damage of institutions dedicated to religion was -- that the accused have no case to answer in respect to that. So I'm just wondering why you're leading now on this. MR. DI FAZIO: I fully accept that evidence - sorry - that finding, if Your Honours please. I have no challenge to it, of course. And I'm aware of it. May I have a brief moment to confer with my colleagues, and I'll put in a reply to your concern in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to abandon this line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I want to ask you some questions regarding cooperation or work with the paramilitaries. You said in cross-examination by Mr. Pantelic that the Crisis Staff did not issue any orders to the army. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the Crisis Staff ever sought to influence army decisions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Crisis Staff was not able to influence the decisions taken by the army in any way. These were two parallel systems, and each had its own sphere of competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if, although the Crisis Staff, you say, was not able to influence the military, whether it sought, it tried to influence the military?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this attempt. An attempt would have to lead to results. I know of no attempts, because then I would also have to know about the responses to such attempts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Tadic, did you ever travel to Belgrade in 1992 in company with Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, Simo Zaric, and Milos -- and meet Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that trip?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already spoken of the problems that occurred in mid-May and a little later; that is, during the second half of May, concerning the constant shelling and the departure of a large number of refugees who were accommodated in Serbia. We have also spoken here about the fact that there were several such transports that were to go to Serbia, and in view of the fact that we had no information from Serbia that they would receive them, because the reception centre was overcrowded, the main purpose was to visit Andjelko Maslic, our fellow townsman who held a high post, so to say, and to see whether there was anything we could do together with him in order to organise several convoys of women, children, and elderly people to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Essentially, is it your position that the trip and the men that I have mentioned was for humanitarian reasons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. That's exactly what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no other purpose at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we set out for Belgrade and saw Andjelko Maslic, there was no other goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that when you set out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you are aware, are you not, that Mr. Zaric was interviewed by officers of the Office of the Prosecution, the Prosecutor, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting my colleague. For a moment I was listening to the witness very carefully, and the answer on page 7, line 8 was -- maybe I'm wrong. I think I heard that it was actually the witness said: "What was that?" something like that. And now I see: "That's correct." MR. DI FAZIO: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should go through this again. It would be maybe the best. I'm not suggesting anything, but ... MR. DI FAZIO: Sure. Very well

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: When you set out for Belgrade in company with those men, you knew that the goal of the trip was purely humanitarian -- was for purely humanitarian reasons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you know that Mr. Zaric has provided interviews to the Office of the Prosecutor and that he was interviewed in 1998, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says here, then that's certainly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in one of those interviews conducted on the 1st of April, 1998, Mr. Zaric was questioned about this trip to Belgrade, and he gave an account of the purpose of the trip and what happened on the trip, and said that all the men that I've mentioned - you, Blagoje Simic, Simo Zaric, Stevan Todorovic, and Milos Bogdanovic - discussed the appointment of Crni as brigade commander. Do you recall anything like that happening on the trip?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask that the precise part of the interview, that is, the page number, be mentioned. If this has already been tendered into evidence, so that we know what Mr. Zaric actually said, and that this part of the interview be put before Mr. Tadic, as has been done up to now. MR. DI FAZIO: P140 ter, pages 66 onwards, to page 78. If Your Honours please, I don't propose to take Mr. Tadic through that portion of Mr. Zaric's interview word for word. There is no point in the Prosecution's submission. If there's anything that needs to be clarified, Mr. Lukic has the interview. He can easily clarify it in re-examination and can easily point out bits of anything that Mr. Zaric said in those interviews to his client and obtain all the clarification that he needs in re-examination. I want to put the essence of what Mr. Zaric said in the course of that interview in those pages, and I believe that I've done so accurately and honestly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the practice should be that where the document whose contents are being discussed is available and is already an exhibit, it must be put before the witness so that he too can refresh his memory. There may be some other interpretation the witness may have, and he's -- he should be free to put up -- that to the Court. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. Thank you. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P140 ter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, would you please look at P140 ter, and may I ask you to look at page 66, which is where the relevant answers begin. The B/C/S you will find about two-thirds of the way down through P140 ter. And would you read that answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this begin with "yes," the line that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct: "Yes, I think he would become our commander."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yes. Automatically he becomes my commander, our commander. Unfortunately, Crni got support immediately from the Corps Commander, Mr. Dencic, thanks to the intervention of the authorities from Samac. Full stop. Dencic, thanks to the intervention of the authorities of Samac - this sentence is a bit unclear - Dencic was a high-ranking official of the corps command and who was the commander of all of us, of all the units. He was the commander of the East Bosnian Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be better for the witness to read this silently to himself. It is not necessary to tire the interpreters with it. But just for Mr. Tadic to familiarise himself with the content. It's better maybe if he reads it silently to himself. Since the paragraph is rather long. It's half a page long. MR. DI FAZIO: I respectfully entirely agree with what Mr. Lukic says. My purpose is to simply allow Mr. Tadic to acquaint himself with what Mr. Zaric essentially said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- about the trip to Belgrade. That's the sole purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO: And I think the witness can do it by skimming through those pages. It won't take him a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, could I ask you to read, as quickly as you can, what Mr. Zaric had to say about the trip to Belgrade. And you will find it in P140 ter, from about page 66 onwards. Okay? Please inform us when you've had an opportunity to see how he describes, how Mr. Zaric describes the trip and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked through it and I'm familiar with it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Tadic. Now, you will agree with me, won't you, that Mr. Zaric essentially describes a different scenario, namely, that you went to Belgrade, to the MUP, and that you met some generals and that you discussed the appointment of a man named Crni as brigade commander. Essentially, without going into the details, but essentially, that is what he said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your interpretation and the interpretation of Mr. Zaric. I can explain this in my own way. The Prosecution could have asked me about this as well, not only Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Mr. Tadic, I only have one question to ask you, and that's this: Are you aware of any reason why Mr. Zaric would describe, at length, these discussions regarding the appointment of a brigade commander, Crni, a paramilitary, and not make any mention of humanitarian purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that before this, the commander had already been appointed. Before this whole story, the commander had already been appointed, and Dencic had already appointed him. This story has a certain after -- it comes after the appointment of the commander. I do not deny that there are things here that I could tell you about, but my main impression was that the commander had already been appointed when all this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Di Fazio, but pursuant to your question on page 11, lines 1 to 5, where you say about Mr. Zaric describing at length these discussions regarding the appointment of a brigade commander, Crni, a paramilitary, and not make any mention of humanitarian purposes, could you just elaborate very briefly for the Trial Chamber: What exactly do you mean by the latter, "and not make any mention of humanitarian purposes." MR. DI FAZIO: If you read the portion of the interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Because I don't, unfortunately, have it right in front of me at the moment. MR. DI FAZIO: His account, Mr. Zaric's account, as I read that part of the interview, is that they arrived in Belgrade and discussed the appointment of Crni as brigade commander, and this followed upon various negotiations that had taken place in Bosanski Samac. Now, unless I've missed something, I saw nothing in the -- in that account that placed the purpose of the trip to Belgrade as being one of humanitarian -- for humanitarian purposes. And I wondered if there was any reason for that, and that was the purpose of ... Page 67, indeed, as Mr. Weiner points out, Mr. Zaric said, when asked about the trip: "It could have been between the 21st of May and the end of May. Already in the car we were told that all of this was about Crni, and we needed to get to Belgrade to get approval." So that was the purposes of it. So is my point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I will refer back to that page in the exhibit. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maslic, who was the first one we went to see when we arrived in Belgrade, then the incident that has already been mentioned here took place, that is, Mr. Todorovic had issued orders that Mr. Zaric, Mr. Bogdanovic, and I, and some other people, should be arrested at the checkpoint in Gorica, and I think that this statement was mentioned here. And then there was an acrimonious discussion about this. Mr. Blagoje Simic tried to calm things down as far as he could, because all this was taking place in the street. And when the situation calmed down, we went there with a strictly humanitarian purpose, because Andjelko Maslic had nothing to do with the appointment of the commander in Samac. He was purely a civilian and had nothing whatsoever to do with that action. When this action was completed, Mr. Todorovic, since he was driving, took us to the place mentioned here, RPV and so on, with the task of possibly demonstrating his position with these -- there was no other purpose to this, because the commander had already been appointed. When we arrived in RPV, the brigade commander was already Crni. We could have tried to strengthen this position, but he had already been appointed and approved by Mr. Dencic as the brigade commander. At this meeting, Mr. Todorovic acted arrogantly. He acted as if he knew everyone. He addressed everyone by their names. We kept quiet because we had seen these people for the first time and we were there for the first time. He was trying to create the impression that he had connections with generals and the people who were present there, three or four people who were there, and in view of the fact that this was a very unpleasant situation and I wasn't even interested, I asked the gentleman, who was the main general there, whether I could see a relative of mine who was a colonel in the air force, whether I could go and see him, because he had uncles in Novi Grad, in the situation that has already been mentioned here, so I won't go into it now. And he made this possible for me. I went out. I met this relative of mine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you need this evidence. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't. I don't need this evidence at all. I just didn't want to prevent Mr. Tadic from providing his full explanation of what occurred at the meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, may I ask you: During the course of the meeting in Belgrade, do you recall Blagoje Simic telephoning and speaking to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I haven't finished my story. I left the room and I went to see the relative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, this is a criminal trial, and the Prosecution is cross-examining you. The Prosecution is only interested in certain parts of everything that you know, because the Prosecution can only elicit evidence relevant to the case. So please do listen to the questions and simply answer them. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, don't worry. You have your counsel, who will clarify anything that you want in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's watching us like a hawk and will make sure that he clarifies anything that I have left unclear. So I put your mind at rest, okay. My only question to you about this meeting is this: In the course of the meeting, did Blagoje Simic speak over the telephone to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the room all the time, but while I was there, and after I came back, no, he didn't. I was there a little bit at the beginning, and then a little bit at the end. During the time I was in the room, he didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to, as briefly as possible, just tell the Chamber, in bullet-point form, in the form of topics only, topics only, what humanitarian activities the four of you -- five of you undertook once you had arrived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't undertake any humanitarian activities. We only told Mr. Maslic about the humanitarian situation on the ground and our wish to try to set up more reception centres for people from Samac. We asked him to undertake some of these activities and to assist us in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, there's no reason, as far as you're aware, for Mr. Zaric to have fabricated any conversation as far as you're aware, between Blagoje Simic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is not a fair question, Mr. Di Fazio, and I will not allow it, in view of the previous answer of the witness -- the accused, rather. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blagoje Simic report to you any conversation that he had had with General Mladic? You may not have heard it, but did he report any such conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our return from Samac, in the car, the atmosphere was very tense, for various reasons. Nobody talked to anyone. Blagoje Simic didn't tell me, then or later, that there had been any conversation with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand your position now. Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber what humanitarian concerns Stevan Todorovic pursued in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the driver. He drove the car. We were there with him and he was there with us, when we went to see Mr. Maslic. He wasn't engaged in humanitarian work, but he drove the car that we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So Mr. Todorovic, chief of police and Crisis Staff member, was purely a chauffeur on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. That's a bit exaggerated, Mr. Di Fazio. That's not what the accused has said. He simply said he drove the car, he didn't say he was purely a chauffeur. That's not fair. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything other than drive the car?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He drove a police car. He was wearing a police uniform and he was able to pass through every checkpoint without any delays. That was his advantage in relation to all civilians, other civilians who might be driving, and it was in his interest to take us to RPV. Had I been driving, I wouldn't have wanted to go to RPV. I had no interest in going there. But as he was driving, he said he had to go there. He had to see his best man, and we couldn't go hitchhiking, so we had to sit in the car and go with him. Milos Bogdanovic didn't make use of this, because he had no obligations towards Todorovic. He had his own car, so he didn't go to RPV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally on this topic: How long did the trip take?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day. We set out in the morning and we came back in the late afternoon. I don't know how long it took, but we stayed perhaps an hour with Maslic, and less than an hour in RPV. And what I know, we quarrelled there for about half an hour in the street about the checkpoint where we were to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Tadic, is it your position that detainees in Bosanski Samac who were exchanged did so voluntarily? I think that's capable of a yes or no answer, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did this voluntarily, at their own wish, and those who didn't wish to do this, they chose the other option and they weren't exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Civilians who were exchanged did so voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're mixing in civilians and exchanges. We said that civilians went to these exchanges. That was the word used, because they had to fulfil certain conditions. They had to have lists, they had to pass through certain checkpoints, they had to be accepted. So that there were a lot of problems there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this way: Is it your position that at the points of exchange, civilians decided to leave voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians were first registered with the Red Cross, and once they put their signature there, and once they provided their own personal information, all sorts of personal information, they would thereby opt to go to be exchanged. But at the line of separation, where they crossed to the other side, they were asked again and they would have to say again, wherever this was possible, wherever this could be arranged, and mostly it could be arranged. I was referring to an exchange on the 13th of January, 1993, when I was not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is that agreement with the proposition that at the points of exchange, those locations, civilians voluntarily left?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, they left of their own free will. They would go to the Red Cross and provide the Red Cross with their personal information, which means that the whole thing was entirely voluntary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know and you agree, don't you, that mass arrests of non-Serbs took place in Bosanski Samac after April 16 and 17?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I just can't agree with the adjective you're using, "mass arrests." If only one, two or three such persons were arrested, I don't think you can call it mass arrests, exactly. So I do agree that there were arrests, yes, but not mass arrests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that large numbers of non-Serb men were arrested after the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday or the day before yesterday, I thought we made it sufficiently clear. In the SUP, in the TO, in the elementary school building, the secondary school building, we even discussed numbers, so I'm not sure there's any need for us to go through these same figures again. I do agree that there were arrests, and as I said the last time I spoke about this, I'm not sure about the specific numbers in some of the places you're referring to, but yes, a number of people were arrested. I believe I said 50 or 60 at the elementary school building at one point in time there were as many as 300 people. I did say this yesterday or the day before yesterday. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. MR. DI FAZIO: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P138 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. While the document is being found. Mr. Tadic, given your background with civilian protection and also with the Red Cross and so on, these people who were detained in the detention centres in Bosanski Samac, would some of them have been classified as prisoners of war under the Geneva Conventions, if you know, given your background in the Red Cross and civilian protection and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably those who were in possession of weapons, those who resisted, or those who had caused other kinds of incidents in the sense you're talking about would have been detainees. But as far as I remember, one of the agreements between the warring sides - I can't remember the specific article - it reads, however, that every person detained, on any grounds, during the conflict is considered a prisoner. I can't quote this off the top of my head right now, but probably the Chamber will get to see this document eventually, so you will be able to check for yourselves. I think that's how this particular part was classified by the agreement signed in Geneva. I really regret very much not having the document before me right now, so I could provide further comments. So the Geneva Conventions were sort of applied with some latitude, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. May I ask you to look at page 40 of P138 ter. I want to just clarify this use of the adjective that you disagree with, namely, "mass arrests." Page 40, please. At the bottom of the page you will see a short, brief paragraph consisting of five lines. Can you please slowly read that into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the part beginning with "no"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "No. I spoke about the first days of the war, which means the 18th, perhaps the 19th and the 20th of April. This implies 1992. I spoke about those days of the war, and I don't know the exact number of people who were arrested then, but certainly no more than 30 persons. The arrest you are speaking about only occurred much later, perhaps as much as a month later." I think this is probably the passage you were referring to. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to -- I'd like you, if you may, Mr. Tadic, to read out loud the last sentence of that -- the last sentence of that answer, clearly and slowly for the interpreters. The last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Start afresh.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So after the full stop: "The arrest you are speaking about only occurred much later, perhaps a month after the event." Is this consistent with the English interpretation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, whatever adjective you care to use, we agree, don't we, that large numbers of non-Serb men were arrested after the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did even go so far as to say but not more than 30 people, so speaking of those first days. That's my conviction. But now you're trying to get me to answer something that I simply can't answer because I don't know. But I should assume that up to 30 people had been arrested on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following that, large numbers of Croat and Muslim men were arrested; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a month after that event. That's what it says here: Perhaps a month after the event. That means after the 18th, 19th, and 20th, a month later there were arrests on a more massive scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So we agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I was just going to say, I'm not going to bother flicking back on the LiveNote here, but I think we've heard Mr. Tadic say now several times that there were approximately 30 people in the first couple of days, and then following that, there were anywhere up to 300 or whatever. It doesn't seem to be a point of contention. MR. DI FAZIO: No. No, no. I think we've arrived at the point where I entirely agree with what Your Honour says. I agree there's no more contention. Mr. Tadic describes arrests on a more massive scale, and indeed I was referring to the English translation of the interview which uses that particular adjective, which was not agreed with at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you knew that these detainees had been tortured and beaten regularly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I tried to answer your question yesterday. If you want me to repeat my answer, I may leave out a word or two that I used yesterday. I'm not sure if this really matters. But I can try to reiterate my answer if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you knew, from hearing conversations in public places, that the prisoners were tortured and beaten regularly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did get to learn, but I wouldn't say regularly. I got to learn from people who did have contact with those prisoners. You have already heard in this discussion that the Red Cross did indeed go to those premises, and quite often. Physicians would go there, and I was in touch with all these people, and they're the only people I could possibly have heard this from, or possibly from a number of police officers that I used to see quite a lot of also and was on friendly terms with, because the police officers I'm talking about were police officers from the former times. So that's what my information was based on, and that's what you heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men who were arrested were arrested by force, that is, at gun point, at their homes and at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were detained against their will?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They weren't free to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I know nothing about that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were kept under guard at the TO, the high school gym, the primary school gym, the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were being held by force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there were guards there, yes, I suppose you could say that they were held there. Now, whether by force or not, I think you should talk to the guards about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The result was, wasn't it, that hundreds of non-Serb men, Croats and Muslims, were being held and separated from the wider community? That stands to reason.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about that. I know that a number of persons were detained, but I don't know any of the other specifics related to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only way out for these men in custody was to leave Bosanski Samac at the point of exchange, where the exchanges took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the ways out, but not the only way out. You have heard testimony here telling you that people were leaving in different ways, in other ways too. This was only one of the ways for these people to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the detainees too, detainees, prisoners, whatever you choose to call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The main way for them to exit their prisons was via an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of, one of the possible ways, was to leave via an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the main way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let us agree that it was the main way, if you view the other ways people leaving as subsidiary ways, then this would probably be the main way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were exchanged for Serbs who came into the territory of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were prisoners, they came for prisoners, mainly Serbs, from the Odzak area. If they were civilians, they would just cross to the other side, to the Croatian side, the Croatian Defence Council. Serb civilians from that side crossed to the Samac area, and from there, some of them remained in the Samac area but some of them travelled on to other areas where they thought it would be easier for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but the result was that they were exchanged for Serbs that came into the territory of Bosanski Samac, territory held by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The result of that was that the ethnic groups were being separated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I know what you mean by "separated." Those who arrived were with those who were in Samac, and those who left were with those who just happened to be there. At that time in Samac, there were all the different ethnic groups, and in the other area too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The process of exchanging non-Serbs for Serbs via exchanges resulted in Serbs leaving the area of Bosanski Samac -- sorry -- non-Serbs leaving the area of Bosanski Samac and Serbs entering it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And large numbers of the non-Serbs leaving Bosanski Samac were those who had been held in detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were in detention centres, but the majority of them were not in any Detention Centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is ethnic separation by force, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, Biljana Plavsic has pleaded guilty to one count of the crime of persecution and is to be sentenced on Thursday. She has admitted to a number of issues and matters, including this: "The SDS and the Bosnian Serb leadership were committed to a primary goal that all Serbs in the former Yugoslavia would remain in a common state. One method of achieving this goal was by separating the ethnic communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. By October 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mrs. Plavsic, knew and intended that the separation of the ethnic communities would include the permanent removal of ethnic populations, either by agreement or by force, and further knew that any forcible removal of non-Serbs from Serbian-claimed territories would involve a discriminatory campaign of persecution. The intention to separate the ethnic communities by force, which included the knowledge that forcible, permanent removal of non-Serb from Serbian-claimed territories would include a discriminatory campaign of persecution is hereinafter referred to as the object of ethnic separation by force." That is what is occurring, is it not, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to comment on a statement like this, but whatever Biljana Plavsic has admitted to, she must be made to answer for. I myself am no lawyer, so I find it difficult to comment. But as a professor of engineering, my comment would probably be a bit different. If Biljana indeed admitted that she had expelled 45.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "4.000"] non-Serbs from our area, the area that we are now referring to, and about a thousand persons left via the exchanges, when non-Serbs were being exchanged, then this would amount to 2 per cent. And if you divide these two per cent up to Veljo Maslic and Miroslav Tadic, then I myself deserve 7 per cent of these 2 per cent. So I don't think it's much of a sin really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript. It should read 40.000 instead of 4.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 45.000 here. What I can see here in the transcript is 4.000. I would not like to comment on Biljana's admission, not being a lawyer myself, but not even as a citizen, it would not be becoming of me to comment on that, because the comment would not be a very favourable one. So I would like to ask you to please spare me that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm not going to invite you just to comment, give us your comments. I'll be fair and I'll ask you very specific questions about it. Okay. I only have one more paragraph that I want to put to you, and then I'll ask you, not for comment, but a specific question, okay? "In addition, the SDS prepared and distributed written instructions to SDS municipal leaders to form Crisis Staffs, proclaim Serbian Municipal Assemblies, and carry out preparations for the formation of municipal governmental bodies and to mobilise Bosnian Serb police and Territorial Defence forces and subordinate them to JNA command. The municipal crisis staffs implemented these objectives and directives in the field, including ultimately the objective of ethnic separation by force." That's what she said in the course of admitting her crime. So she has admitted to pursuing ethnic separation and by force, and she has said that the municipal crisis staffs had an important role to play. Do you agree with her assessment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with her assessment. First of all, I never saw Biljana Plavsic anywhere within 20 kilometres from where I was. I only saw her a couple of times on TV, when she was giving a speech. I never saw her own papers, her documents, the ones you're talking about here that she had given the orders or devolved these orders onto lower levels of decision making. Therefore, I'm not in agreement with her assessment, at least as concerns this particular section of her assessment, even if I never said that I was not to blame for anything. But these particular issues that Biljana Plavsic is here referring to, I really have nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She has said that she participated in the giving of instructions to carry out these policies, including the objective of ethnic separation by force. You were a member of such a Crisis Staff, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a brief while, for a very brief while, I was a member of such a Crisis Staff, and I said what the reason was, and I also said clearly that this Crisis Staff never received any document coming from Biljana Plavsic, speaking about this. The Crisis Staff never received any discriminatory documents from anyone else either. The Crisis Staff never issued any papers or documents inciting to discrimination in the sense being discussed. If what Biljana Plavsic is saying now were true, I'm sure the Dayton Accords would never have been reached, and the Republika Srpska would probably now not have its own borders, its own president, its own police force, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic has said that instructions came from the Bosnian Serb leadership, not just herself. Did not such instructions from the Bosnian Serb leadership come to the Crisis Staff of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I have never seen any of those leaders or members of that leadership anywhere near where I was, except on TV, and I have never seen a letter or an order inciting to discrimination signed by anyone, Biljana Plavsic or any of the other leaders for that matter. Myself, I was not that high-ranking an official, nor was my interest really that catholic [Realtime transcript read in error "Catholic"], so I was not really in touch with the people that you have been referring to. Samac, as a place, was quite far away from the events, from the events that are under discussion here, from Biljana Plavsic and from the other people too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. I think this is probably something in translation. Page 28, line 9, when Mr. Tadic says "his interest really wasn't that Catholic," I presume it's use of the word "Catholic," meaning universal, rather than Catholic as a religion as such. MR. DI FAZIO: That's a legitimate meaning of the word, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you described -- when you described your interest not really that catholic I take it you mean universal, all-encompassing, something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never meant Catholic in the sense of religion, and I don't think any such meaning could have been gleaned from the context, the context that I was talking about. I wasn't talking about the Catholic church, Catholic as in the Catholic church. I meant universal or far-ranging. I was not referring to Catholics or Muslims or Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P162 ter. If Your Honours please, this was produced by Witnesses DW 1/3. I want to inquire as to whether or not it's under seal. I just want to make sure it's not under seal before it's produced.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is under seal. MR. DI FAZIO: It is under seal. I'd ask that the appropriate measures be taken for -- to make sure that it's protected and -- is it necessary for us to go into closed session, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It depends on the questions you ask. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I won't be asking about the content of the document, so it might be safe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we'll go into private session. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Di Fazio, would you allow me to read one more sentence? MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. I don't want to muzzle the witness or to be seen to muzzle the witness. Perhaps we can go back into private session, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Because he wants to read from the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't have to be in private session. From this statement, yes, but it doesn't mention the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Can you wait? We'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, your position has been that the Crisis Staff did not involve itself in the actual organisation and running of the exchanges; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at this document that I've produced to you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, copies were served on the Defence well over a week ago, and I have sufficient English copies and B/C/S copies of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, two questions: Is that your signature on the document and are you familiar with that document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature, and I am familiar with the document, and I, a few days ago, I explained how this document came to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Tadic. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, I seek to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P163 and P163 ter for the B/C/S. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is that portion of the document that is covered by your signature true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what it says here, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that what it says is it. My question is: Is the content of the document to which you appended your signature true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document refers to agreement between Red Crosses, as well as Crisis Staffs; therefore, Crisis Staffs negotiated and participated in the agreement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that this is the way I drew up the document in order to obtain the approval of the people mentioned here. I said I went to Belgrade to organise this exchange in July 1992, and when I arrived there, the people from the commission of Yugoslavia told me I had to have a document, on the basis of which I could ask for approval to enter Yugoslavia, to enter the UNPA zone, and to address the UNPROFOR in Belgrade. I said to him: "I don't have any documents." And the man said to me: "What are you doing? Do you have an Exchange Commission?" I said: "Well, formally we are working, but we have no commission." He said: "What do you do?" I said I was the head of the civilian protection staff. He asked me: "Is there a civilian body?" I said: "Well, there's a Crisis Staff." So then let's put down a request on behalf of the Crisis Staff to give this some weight. And then the man drew up this document. He had never even been to Samac or seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. The document says: "In accordance with agreement reached between Red Cross and Crisis Staffs." Therefore, the Crisis Staffs entered into negotiations regarding the agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you expecting an answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that this is only the way the letter was drafted, on the basis of which letter I was supposed to receive approval. You see who the addressees are and who the letter was sent to. This was not written by the Crisis Staff. This has never undergone any kind of protocol. There is no signature on behalf of the Crisis Staff. It means on behalf of the Crisis Staff, Miroslav Tadic. So I signed this on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence. It says: "The Crisis Staff requests the approval and assistance in order to realise this exchange." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. What do you think, if I had written Miroslav Tadic seeks your approval? What would the UNPROFOR people have said? What institution are you to seek approval? So you had to seek approval on somebody's behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question -- my question is this: It says the Crisis Staff requests your approval and assistance. Is it true -- to realise the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it reads, but there is also the explanation that if I take upon myself the obligation that I did this, is there any problem with that? The Crisis Staff did not know about this, nor were they the ones who wrote this document. I wrote the document myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Tadic, at the time you signed this particular document, P163, were you actually a member of the Crisis Staff at that point in time, the period in time that this was signed and leading up to the exchange in Lipovac on Saturday, 11th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was a little earlier than what it actually states, the 11th of July. There is no date here when it was written because an exchange was organised for the 11th of July, and actually it was held on the 5th of July. I'm not sure how many days in advance this was written, but the form and the content and the purpose of this letter is what I've just explained. Approval was needed from UNPROFOR, from Yugoslavia, or from the Krajina, for that matter, for us to pass through the area. I had no experience at that point as to how to go about this, because I was in Belgrade for the first time, meeting the people who are mentioned here: General Radinovic, who was the president of Yugoslavia's commission, and he backed my letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. But to answer my question sort of succinctly: When you signed it, obviously you recall signing it, because you've said that, when you signed it, when you actually, at that point in time, a member of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at that time it was still Crisis Staff, but that was towards the end. But I think at that point there was still such a thing as the Crisis Staff. Perhaps I would have written War Presidency if it was already War Presidency. But you had to sign someone here, the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency. But I think at this point in time it was still the Crisis Staff. I had to -- I sent this document to Mario Velikonja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just to follow up again, just for clarity: And at that time you were a member of the Crisis Staff as it then was, before it became the War Presidency? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tadic. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, Witness Q testified that he was informed the night before his exchange that he would be exchanged and that he suffered continuous beating and torture during the period of his incarceration. You recall that evidence, that unchallenged evidence? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't challenged, and I won't challenge it myself. I'm not sure who Witness Q is. I can't remember at the moment. But if he said that there was beating, I have no reason to say that there wasn't simply because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should not bring the witness -- we should not mislead the witness. We should go into private session, and I think the Prosecutor should put the name of the witness to Mr. Tadic in order to refresh his memory. So maybe if we could just have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution pressing this? MR. DI FAZIO: I've got the answer I want. If Defence counsel is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Especially that the beatings are not being contested. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. They're not being contested. Thank you. I don't press for the matter to go into private session, no. I'd like to proceed, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you would agree that that person had no choice but to leave through the exchange?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you're continually referring to Q, we had better have his name so Mr. Tadic can be reminded. I thought you weren't continuing with reference to Witness Q

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Lukac gave evidence, unchallenged evidence, of being arrested, tortured, detained, moved from prison to prison, and asked by Sveto Vasovic, the night before his exchange, if he wanted to be exchanged. He had no choice but to be exchanged. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, many other people opted to be exchanged, many other people who had choice. I'm not saying that Lukac was or was not in a position to choose between leaving and staying, but the witness you have referred to before, and Lukac, they were all able to say: We refuse to go away. We'll go back to Samac. The witness you referred to before. I even believe that he was able to go back to Samac, because he was well regarded among the people in Samac. Lukac also would have been able to return, but he didn't think that that was the best option for him, so he decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muhamed Bicic testified, unchallenged, that he was beaten and tortured repeatedly, including being tortured by a member of the Crisis Staff. That evidence was unchallenged. He testified he was taken from the TO to the primary school, without any consultation whatsoever, and exchanged. No one even bothered to ask him. That evidence was unchallenged. He had no choice but to be exchanged, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that he was never asked, but in any case, had he wanted to, he would been able to go home, repair his pizzeria, the pizzeria that he used to own, if not at the same time as all the others, then perhaps a while later, because that's what many other people did. So we can't generalise like that: They could or they couldn't. Some people chose to go and some people chose to stay. It's as simple as that. We have people on the both sides who are still alive, people who at one point chose to go, and people who at one point chose to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness N was also a victim of Milan Simic. He was repeatedly tortured, had his teeth pulled out with pliers, I believe had a half moon carved into his head with a knife. He was exchanged. He didn't have any choice to be exchanged, did he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same rule applies to all of them. If he had stayed, if he had returned, I believe that very soon he would have been able to press charges, if not immediately, at a later stage, he could have pressed charges, he would have been in a position to press charges for everything that was done to him, and I'm sure that there would have been a trial, as there have been other trials. We do not have any interest or use, if these people know who they had been carved up by, who had extracted their tooth, then they go somewhere far away and from a distance of 5.000 kilometres they talk about someone having extracted their tooth. If this dentist is still around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, control. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You need those answers? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't -- I'm not unhappy with the answers, if Your Honours please, but I have to tread a delicate line between trying to muzzle the witness and control him. However, I understand from Your Honours are saying and I will endeavour to ensure that the answers are not too rambling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Could I just ask one small question before you begin, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Tadic, with several of the witnesses whose names or numbers I don't recall right now, we heard that there was really no possibility during the period of April, May, June 1992, and maybe longer, to bring cases before civilian, civil, or criminal courts. So I'm just wondering, with respect to your answer that some of these persons Mr. Lukac and others, Mr. Bicic, and so on, that had they decided not to be exchanged and would have simply stayed in Samac, how they would have got the remedy at that point in time rather than going across the separation line, if they had decided to stay, when Mr. Todorovic was still in power as chief of police and so on. I wonder whether you might have some comments on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they had stayed, Mr. Todorovic would have been removed much sooner than he eventually was, in all likelihood. That's one thing. Secondly, we've heard testimonies before this Court to the effect that certain trials had already begun, if you remember the case of Goran Kljajic. Certain cases were brought before tribunals. Those were isolated cases, for the simple reason that many of these people now reside very far from Samac, so therefore, they decide not to bring these cases. We heard about one man having two or three of his teeth pulled out, and another had four of his teeth pulled out, and all these people are alive and well, but somewhere else, but they choose not to bring any cases before the local tribunals because they live far away. But they would be able to do so, if they chose to do so. So now they're trying to shift the blame to me for all these people who extracted other people's teeth, for all these people who beat other people. Me, and I'm completely blameless in this. So I'm going to have to take the blame for all of those people who had done such things. And even here, we've had witnesses who spoke about spending time together with those beaters and with those dentists, in a manner of speaking, and about preparing new beatings and new tooth extractions together with those people. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, did you or the Exchange Commission, or at any time in 1992, make inquiries of these people as to whether or not they wanted to cross over?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been compelled to repeat this several times already. All of those people volunteered, registered with the Red Cross, and said that they wanted to go. Others, at the separation line, said clearly whether they wanted to go or not. Unfortunately, we've spoken about a number of exchanges. For example, 26 Serbs came from Orasje who were supposed to cross over to our side. Only six of them said they actually wanted to cross over to the Serbian side, and 20 of them eventually returned to Orasje. So there was no exception there. People thought it was time they went back to where they came from and to try to do their best to create better living conditions where they belong. And this is very much what happened in Samac. People who returned or those who refused to be exchanged struggled to reach a certain position, and they eventually succeeded. They continued their lives like everybody else. Nowadays they have a perfectly normal life. Yes, they did have a hard time, but that applied to everyone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Tadic. Snjezana Delic testified, unchallenged that she had lived in Bosanski Samac all her life, that she met her husband Dragan Delic and married in 1979, had two kids, a boy and a girl, aged 10 and 7 in 1992, and that she taught economics at the secondary school until April of 1992. You recall that evidence, don't you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Delic testified that he lived most of his life in Bosanski Samac, he was president of the managing board of Mebos in 1992, and that both he and his wife, Snjezana, were exchanged on the 4th of September, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, in case you got all the dates right, yes, that should be correct. Yes, they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rely on me, Mr. Tadic. Snjezana Delic testified that she couldn't get money out of a bank account following the arrest of her husband. That evidence was unchallenged; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I also told you what happened to my bank account, so we were in the same position, because we were both private entrepreneurs. I couldn't get any of my money out at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She testified that she couldn't get money out of her bank account following the arrest of her husband and that it was because the arrest of her husband that she was unable to get her money out; correct? That evidence was unchallenged. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not arrested, and it seems I was quite Serb in a manner of speaking for not being arrested. And yet I was not able to get any of my money out from the account, from any of the accounts. I enumerated most of them, and I still don't have any of that money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, with respect, I am not asking you about your bank accounts. I'm asking you about the testimony of Snjezana Delic. She testified that she couldn't get money out of a bank account following the arrest of her husband, for that reason. That testimony was unchallenged by your counsel; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason for me not to believe what Snjezana said. I myself was not able to do that. Why would she have been able to do so and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We've heard enough about your own problem on this. Just answer the question put to you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll finish quickly, Mr. Tadic, if we keep the answers short, I can guarantee that. Snjezana Delic testified that a curfew was imposed but that Serbs could move around as they wished. That was unchallenged; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this whole line of questioning is really about two questions. The witness should be asked if he knows whether his Defence or any other Defence ever challenged the fact so he can say what he thinks about it. But we have the same questioning recurring all the time. The witness is supposed to tell us whether he knows whether any of the Defence teams had ever challenged the fact. So it's all about these two questions: Whether this is indeed true or whether any of the Defence teams had ever challenged the fact. All these facts have indeed been challenged by the Defence, especially what we are talking about now, during cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Snjezana Delic testified that a curfew was imposed but that Serbs could move around as they wished. Your counsel did not challenge that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, if I recall correctly, at the very beginning of this trial, there was a discussion about this, whether if another counsel asked a question, the other counsel should repeat. I remember this. And we avoided repetition of similar questions by different counsel. So it's not fair to put it that way. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll leave the curfew, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Snjezana Delic testified that she lost her job as a teacher. Any reason to disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason. When the war began, the elementary school ceased to operate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Snjezana Delic testified that the police were looking for her brother following April of 1992. Any reason to disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to either agree or disagree. I simply don't remember about her brother, and I do not know who her brother is. But I believe she said before this Tribunal that Serbs had taken, via Belgrade, into Serbia. I think that's what she said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Snjezana Delic testified that she had an opportunity to see the mass arrests of Croat and Muslim men. Any reason to challenge that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we're going back to the discussion of mass arrests. We've been through that I think more than twice. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours pleases, I've got a few more questions to get to a particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but don't repeat matters that have been discussed before. Please avoid that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the mass murders of detainees at Crkvina was a matter that was commonly known; correct? You can answer that with a simple yes or a no, I assure you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most people knew. I can't say everyone knew. My own child, for example, didn't know, so what exactly do we imply when we say "everyone knew"? Most of those who knew, knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit P124, the gazette, the attention I drew you to, resulted in the disenfranchisement of Croats and Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was that disenfranchised the Croats and Muslims. I don't think there is any inherent logic in the question. The information on Crkvina, do you mean that that in some way disenfranchised them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, Croats and Muslims no longer had their representatives at body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Isn't this a repetition of -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it is a repetition, please, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm not allowing it. That's all. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Snjezana Delic have a choice in whether she remained or was exchanged in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did have a choice. She was able to stay. But her husband decided to go, so probably she followed her husband. She testified before this Tribunal that she had no work obligation, that she was at home, that she was receiving humanitarian aid, as all other citizens. Her husband was in detention. He opted to go and she accepted that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in re-direct, if I may, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, I just want to clarify a few points. My learned friend Mr. Di Fazio asked you some questions about the work of the multiparty local assembly in Samac before April 1992, after the elections of 1990 an assembly was constituted. Do you know that from the end of 1991 until April 1992, in the local parliament or assembly of Samac, there was outvoting and the work was being blocked? Did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it through the media. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to that question. It doesn't arise at all from the questioning that I conducted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: From the cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: From the cross-examination. My cross-examination on the topic was simply the existence of those bodies, not its functionings, and now Mr. Pantelic is going into that particular topic. It simply didn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is exactly the point. I'm grateful to my learned friend that he actually confirmed my position. His question was strictly related to the functioning of the multiparty Samac local assembly, and I just want to clarify this issue. We all know that -- MR. DI FAZIO: No. My questions were not relating to the actual functioning of the body. My questions were relating to the existence of that body. I did not go into its work, into its activities, between 1991 and 1992, so the question does not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, maybe that's a kind of the game of the words. Existence is one thing and the functioning -- maybe it's a question of understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. The point is clear. If you're talking about existence that they were established, as to whether or not they carried out any functions or made, for instance, is another point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that sense --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question was related to that sense, yes. I will try to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, did you know anything at the time about the fact that the commander of the Territorial Defence and the chief of police were appointed contrary to the legislation then in force? We are talking about April 1992. Did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I mean, I heard about the changes. I don't know whether they were lawful or not. I didn't go into that. It was a relatively brief period of time and I didn't know anything special about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next topic, Mr. Tadic, or rather, the next topic broached by the Prosecution, refers to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, and it is connected to the previous topic of the functioning of the assembly.
