On the 17th, 18th, and 19th of April, the 20th of April, or rather, the first week after the 17th of April, did you see Mr. Mato Nujic around town, a Croat, who was the president of the previous Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see Mr. Mato Nujic, either on the 16th or in the days before or after that date. I didn't see him in that period at all, in those five or six days before the 16th, or after the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tadic: As for some other important people whom you probably knew and who are Croats, did you see them in the period after the 17th of April, 1992, in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before and after the 16th, I didn't move around a lot, and I didn't see them, but I'm sure that after the 16th they were no longer in Samac. They left before the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could you just bear with me for a second, because my co-counsel just informed me that something in the transcript is not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Just a correction for the transcript. It's page 55, in my question between lines 11 and 13, I mentioned also the other functioner Croat by nationality, local functioner, the name is Mato Majanovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him either, although I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another question in line 24 for the court recorder. Mr. Madjarevic, something like that. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said, in response to certain questions by my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio, concerning the functioning of another municipality in 1992 and 1993, and that is Samac Domaljevac. That's another municipality in Samac. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only want to know whether you have any personal knowledge as to whether the municipality of Samac Domaljevac had a Crisis Staff in that period.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same in every municipality. You have heard here that even villages had them. We heard a witness here, one that we have mentioned just a while ago, who said that the village of Tisina also had a Crisis Staff, so that every village, small or large, had this form of authority. They all had their crisis staffs, so the same goes for Samac Domaljevac. If I remember rightly, a man called Coskovic was the secretary, or something or other, in the municipality of Samac, and then he went over to the municipality of Domaljevac Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. While we are on this topic, do you have any personal knowledge about the functioning of the crisis staffs, that is, when and under what conditions they were established? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- this certainly did not arise in cross-examination at all, directly or indirectly. It's an entirely fresh and new topic. The functioning of crisis staffs outside of Samac, that didn't -- simply didn't arise. It simply did not arise at all in any sense, directly or indirectly, and it's entirely a new topic and we should leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you questions about civilian protection, where you had a certain post, and you explained the protection of buildings with sandbags and so on and so forth. Can you tell us whether, in 1992 and 1993, or rather, how often Samac was shelled in this period, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that Samac was shelled very often, sometimes twice a day, sometimes every other day, sometimes three times a day, and sometimes not. I can tell you that for three years my wife slept in the basement. For three years she was in the basement. She would never sleep in the bedroom, although I did. But she was so afraid of the shelling, and that was because shells fell daily. At least 20 shells landed close to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correction to the transcript. The witness was referring to his wife's sister and not his wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was talking about my wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with a topic broached by the Prosecution, that is, the detention centres in the schools and the Territorial Defence, do you know when these detention centres in Samac stopped operating?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I think I'll stop you, because you're now going into the general evidence. You're not dealing with matters strictly dealing with your client's defence which might have been raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my basis for this question was simply to see when -- while we are still on the topic of civilian protection staff and activities, when in fact in Samac these detention centres were dismantled or abandoned or transferred, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying is that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Strictly, Your Honour, related to the civilian protection staff, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying is: Is does not concern strictly your client, so this is a matter which Mr. Lukic, if he wishes to, should be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Your Honour. I will follow that instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to put questions to you about Biljana Plavsic's statement to the Prosecution. You were also asked questions concerning the Official Gazette and the deputies in the Municipal Assembly, and so on. Mr. Tadic, do you have any knowledge of whether, in the SDS in Samac, there were also non-Serbs by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was not in the immediate vicinity, I cannot remember whether there were any non-Serbs. There may well have been, but I can't think of any right now, because I haven't really thought about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you were not active in the party. That is not in dispute. But you were a man about town, you knew quite a lot of people. Darko Dujmusic, a Croat, do you know that he was a member of the SDS? MR. DI FAZIO: This is now amounting to cross-examination. The witness has said he doesn't -- he can't remember whether there were any non-Serbs. That's the end of the matter. In my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's jogging his memory, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Pantelic. Will you sit down. Just sit down. Let Mr. Lukic do the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I ask that document P163 ter be put before the witness Re-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, in your speech, do you use the Ekavian dialect or the Ijekavian dialect, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the Ijekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the word "exchange," do you say razamijama [phoen] or razmena?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say razmena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please read what it says here in the title?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read what it says down here. The army of Yugoslavia for the exchange "razmena" of prisoners. And in other places also, I said that I didn't type out this document; it was done by Mr. Mirko Strbac. That was the man's name. And he typed this out and took it to his boss, and his boss was this general who put a stamp on it, and that's on the basis of this we got approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Page 59, line 22, it should read r-a-z-j-m-e-n-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think on the same note, if the words are of striking importance, maybe the previous line, unless it will be automatically corrected in the transcript, because you've mentioned two words, and so on. So maybe we should make sure that we get them both clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The correct spelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just as we heard from those witnesses who said they heard people from Serbia speaking. A person from Serbia would say razmena. We Serbia from Bosnia would say razmjena. They would say belo, they would say bijelo. You can see quite clearly that this was typed by someone who is from Serbia and who uses Serbian words. And I explained how this document was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is clear enough now. I think the witness has explained that the whole document is written in a dialect which is Serbian, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is there a stamp of the Crisis Staff on this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only stamp on this document is that of the military commission, General Tadinovic [phoen]. And you can see it down here. And I just scribbled something on behalf of the Crisis Staff to avoid having to go home and ask for a document. So to expedite matters, they helped me by doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time this document was written, and you said it was sometime in July 1992, did the Commission for Exchange in Samac exist formally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. He asked me whether it existed, and I said no, not formally, but we were working on it. We were doing things. And he asked me what I was doing, and when I explained what I was doing, he said: "Well, that's not really the sort of institution that would ask for this approval." So that's how we reached this -- we came to write this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add: "It says Saturday the 11th of July, 1992," and it was because of the problems around the gentleman mentioned here. We changed the date and said the 4th of July in order to avoid the return of Mr. Todorovic, although this was supposed to be on the 11th, we actually carried out the exchange on the 4th. But it had been planned or scheduled for the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of February, in response to the Prosecutor's question as to whether you had a free hand concerning the exchanges, you said -- I won't quote you, but you said you didn't, and you explained why, and you said that had you been able to, you would have exchanged all for all, and everything would have been finished. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know what you meant when you said that the business would have been over, or the job would have been done. What did you mean by your job or your business?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My only wish was to deliver these people from the situation they were in, whatever side they were on. Very little has been said about this here, but now I have an opportunity to say that this was the most humane work to be done at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your job to fulfil the wishes of all those who wanted to cross from one side to the other? Is that how you understood your job?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't ever want something to happen to others that you don't wish to happen to you, and that I fully agree with. Whatever I did to them, I want to be done to me under certain circumstances. The circumstances were what they were, and I did everything in my power, and had I been in their situation, I would have been happy had they done this for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, on the same day, said, when he asked you a question about detention units, whether these were reception centres or camps, and he was referring to the TO, the SUP, the primary school, and the secondary school, and he asked you to say whether you agreed with the statement that this was not the kind of traditional prison that existed in the 1980s and 1990s. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that during the 1970s and 1980s in Samac, and you lived in Samac at that time, that hundreds of pieces of illegal weapons were found? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: This is not -- this is not a topic that arose in cross-examination. The only point of raising the issue of his knowledge of traditional prisons was in fact it arose, from what I recall, from a question from the Bench. It's just to distinguish the normal traditional prison from the institutions that were set up in Bosanski Samac. That was the only point. It was purely a device to clarify the situation in Bosanski Samac, not to -- yes, not to go into the issue of traditional prisons generally, and that's what my friend is doing. The question is: Do you know that during the 1970s and 1980s you lived in Samac, and he's actually putting, as well as the issue not arising, he's actually putting matters to the witness. It's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must explain. What I am about to ask is directly related to the cross-examination, because the first series of questions by the Prosecutor was related to whether detention had been set up because of exchange. And then he followed this by saying that there was no detention -- or detention centres in Samac in the 1970s and 1980s. So now I must clarify what the witness actually understands when he says detention, because that exactly was the Prosecutor's question. The question was whether detention centres were set up for the exchange to take place later on. And if you want me to, I can quote the exact section of the Prosecutor's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I've got no problems with Mr. Lukic seeking clarification of what Mr. Tadic meant by detention centres. I have no particular problem with that question, it's just the embarking into descriptions of traditional prisons from the 1970s and 1980s. It simply doesn't arise. It's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think there's another question, Mr. Lukic, with we haven't heard anything about hundreds of pieces of illegal weapons being found in -- you don't mention whose hands in the 1970s and 1980s. That is clearly not part of the indictment, and certainly to my recollection hasn't been raised in connection with Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the explanation by Mr. Di Fazio is clear, and I would like also to warn Mr. Tadic that because he's listening to this exchange, not to go back to what is not being allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree, Your Honours. I just wanted to clarify the answer which the Prosecution wanted to take for granted as to my client's understanding of what detention centres were and whether there were reasons for such detention centres as qualified by the Prosecution to be set up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, the Prosecution asked you to say whether you did anything on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, when you went through the experience that you had to go through, when you heard sounds of shooting. Your answer was that phone lines were down on that particular night. My question is: Were you trying actually during that night to get in touch with anyone to find out what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio asked me about my being worried. All I can say: Your worry must be proportional to the level of information on the actual events that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The question put to you by Mr. Lukic is clear, and just stick to the question. Just answer the question. You don't have to go back or explain anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we've spoken about a wide range of subjects, both in the examination-in-chief and in the cross-examination. During that night, did you at any point attempt to find out what was going on over the phone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that, and several times. At first, the phone lines just weren't working. The lines were down. I wasn't able to speak to anyone. When phones started working again in the morning, I did ring up several people and I talked to those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was only whether you made any attempts to reach anyone by phone, and when you saw that the phone lines were down, did you still want to find out what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that the phone lines are down unless I try phoning someone. So when I realised that phones weren't working, I still tried several times when the phone lines started working again, I did speak to a friend who lived at the other end of the town and I found out about the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your cross-examination, you said that in the morning you spoke to Commander Antic and that he told you that you needn't come and that he would call you when your presence was required. You repeated this twice, both in the examination-in-chief and in the cross-examination. My question is: The order of a senior officer in the army not to do anything and to wait, is that considered an order as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly an order, because in the army, the rule that everyone adheres to is carry out an order and complain afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you a number of questions resulting from today's cross-examination, and the issue was referred to by Mr. Di Fazio during the cross-examination. He asked you about the arrests. You spoke already about Todorovic informing you of those arrests. My question is specifically: Why were people being arrested, to the best of your knowledge? Why were people detained in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question could best be answered by Todorovic himself, but what I can tell you is now, from this case, I learned most of what I know about the arrests. I don't know why the arrests were made. I suppose because people failed to turn over their weapons, because they kept weapons secretly, because they kept explosives secretly. I think that's as far as I know. I would not dare go as far as to say that people were also arrested for minor infringements, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, do you know that even a single person was arrested in order to simply be exchanged in the territory of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, the people who were arrested had nothing to do with any of the exchanges. They had nothing to do with people from Novi Grad. Therefore, these two just cannot be connected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution asked you today, and asked you to agree, that the only way for persons to escape detention was to -- for them to agree to be exchanged. You said it was one of the ways. My question is the following. We have heard this already in testimonies before this Tribunal, even in your own testimony, but I would like now for this to tie up with the question asked you by the Prosecutor. If any person was granted the right to be exchanged and the person refused, would the person go back to detention?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and we have seen a number of such cases. All those who refused to be exchanged went home. That was the result of the first exchange ever, when the International Red Cross informed us of this obligation, and we complied with it, to the letter. Many of the witnesses have confirmed this. It was not my will for Mr. Borbeli to get off near the church and to go straight home. He knew that from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My following question, related again to the Prosecution question: The release of these persons from detention, was it ever dependent upon their subsequent exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't think I fully understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have a choice? That was my question. They could either, A, go to an exchange; B, go home. So my next question following from this --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could go to an exchange or they could go home, so the choice was up to them what they would do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would they have remained in detention had they refused to go for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, had they not decided to go to an exchange, they would have remained in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was a case brought before a Tribunal and approval granted for a person to be exchanged, you said the police and the competent military organs were in charge of that. That's what you said. And this person was granted approval to go to an exchange. If this person refused to go to an exchange, where would the person go? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't recall there being any reference to any tribunals at all in the course of the cross-examination, and it hasn't arisen in any of the previous answers of the witness in re-examination. It's entirely a new topic, as far as I can see, and there's been no explanation of it or how it arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't really -- this question was not addressed to the Tribunal. MR. DI FAZIO: No. I understand that. He's talking -- Mr. Lukic is talking about some sort of courts or tribunals, I believe. In addition to the objections that I just mentioned, I also object on the basis that it is a highly leading question. It's putting the answer straight into the mouth of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, my question was: Why were people being arrested? And you said that people were arrested because of suspicion that they had committed illegal acts. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going any further into this. I just wanted to quote. My question is very simple: Could anyone go to an exchange without previously receiving permission, approval, from the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've ascertained that a couple of times. They couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the exchange of a certain person was approved that the person could go and be exchanged, could they of their own free will decide to stay in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people could decide to stay in Samac, but it was common practice that they should go to the separation line, because no one would have believed that the person wanted to stay. People literally had to go as far as the separation line to declare themselves unwilling to leave, and then they would go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was a purely formal thing. But essentially --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, essentially, people would have been allowed to remain in Samac, and some people actually did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, for example, the police approve for a person to go for an exchange and the person refuses, would the police have any right to keep the person in detention?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police can do just about anything, but they shouldn't do just about anything. I don't remember there were any such cases where this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, during the period that you worked on these exchanges, do you know that anyone from the Samac municipal territory was exchanged against their will, that a person wanted to stay, and that despite this, they were exchanged? Have you heard of any such cases occurring?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single one. No one was expelled by force from Samac. All those who left applied to leave of their own free will and eventually left of their own free will, or returned. No one was kept back in Samac either by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was to be my next question. Do you know that anyone in Samac expressed their desire to leave and were forbidden to leave, if all the conditions that you've talked about had been met?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the conditions were met, no one was forbidden to leave. No one was kept back, held back by force in Samac. There were people who met the conditions and yet they decided to stay. They were free to go. They went as far as the separation line, but there they declared themselves unwilling to leave and then they would return to Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The exchanges in which you took part, was the work related to ethnic separation or was this about bringing families back together?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little has been said about the humanitarian aspect of the whole thing here. One of the crucial principles was to bring families back together, and this applied to Croats, Muslims, and Serbs equally. Little has been said about that, about how the sick and the wounded were transferred to the other side. All those people who were transferred from one area to another, there was a possibility for them always at a certain point to return to their own place or town. Not everyone was in a position to take advantage of this right, especially Serbs. They did. We had witness, my witness, who went of his own free will to Gradacac, then he returned, and today he has the same job, the same position as he used to have. He was in a deposition, so we didn't hear much about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can rest assured that the Trial Chamber will study that testimony too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my re-direct examination. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. I just have one small question, Mr. Tadic, just leading on from what Mr. Lukic has been asking you, and I wonder whether, to your knowledge, in connection with your part in the exchanges, whether you know of anyone who had been severely beaten in one of the detention centres, the TO, the SUP, the schools, et cetera, in Bosanski Samac, who went to the line of separation, on the buses and so on, and decided not to be exchanged, was returned back to Bosanski Samac, and was just allowed to go back to his or her apartment or home. Do you know of anybody in that category who had been severely beaten, who went to the line and returned home and was not detained any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of such details. I can't say that about the people who returned. It's true that people were maltreated to a lesser extent. Those who were maltreated to a greater extent, because of the fear that they acquired, I don't know that any of these people came back. I know that those who were maltreated badly, that these people have not come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, if my memory serves me right, you told us during your testimony that somewhat more than 1.000, either Muslims or, in most cases, Croats, went or left the municipality of Bosanski Samac through the exchange lists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. But there were a lot of people, mostly Croats, I think, but also Muslims, leaving the municipality in other ways, not through the lists, but in other ways. Do you have any, so to say, idea of the number of people leaving in other ways and by other means than through the exchange lists? And as a follow-up question: What was the reason for their leaving the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that the area was affected by war or that the war was very close and later came to the area. I would just like to remind you that many witnesses have already said this here. I won't mention names of witnesses, but one of our last witnesses said that about 400 people from Zasavica, before the 16th of April, at the request of the Odzak Crisis Staff, went over to Odzak, and that about 170 of them remained in Zasavica as a sort of guard or something like that. And I have said that my friend, Pero Tomic, who was a high-ranking official in the HDZ, stayed there. Another witness who was also mentioned here towards the end told us that in his parish there were about four and a half thousand Croats and that before hostilities broke out, about 4.000 of his parishioners left the area and went mostly to Croatia, to the West, to all sorts of places. And he said that about 450 people stayed behind in his parish; that in mid-May, Mr. Braco Blazanovic, who was a teacher of the Serbian-Croatian language, later went to Brod and fell in with a group of armed Croatian soldiers, met the bus, if you remember, and riddled it with bullets. And this witness said that they took about 250 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- took about 250 men away. These are numbers that have been shown here. A witness from Gornji Hasici said that a lot of people left Gornji Hasici before these events, that his entire family - his wife, his children, and everybody else - left and that he remained there on his own in Samac. You have been able see, and I will mention only Sulejman Tihic, who said that his entire family left. Hasan Bicic, Muhamed Bicic, their whole families left. Dragan Lukac, all his family left Samac, and so on and so forth. So that most of the population left before the event that took place between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tadic, I have no wish whatsoever to prolong my questioning, but you are now giving examples about isolated cases comprising, lets say, ten people, a hundred people, and 250 people, and so on. But if I'm correct and my memory serves me right, it's a question of thousands, and perhaps ten thousands of people, leaving the municipality of Samac, after the hostilities broke out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that 4.000 people left. But if you know that the area that was part of the Serbian municipality of Samac did not have the thousands that are mentioned here. The village of Prud, which was once part of the municipality of Samac, had close to 2.000 inhabitants, but it was left out of these events. They didn't go anywhere. Furthermore, Grebnice, a village that also had a large population, Bazik, which also had many inhabitants, and Domaljevac, which was the largest village in Posavina. All these villages remained in the area of the municipality of Samac-Domaljevac, or rather, Domaljevac-Samac. Kornica which also used to belong to Samac and had about 2.000 inhabitants, also at that time did not belong to the Serbian municipality of Samac. I don't want to add these numbers up, but if we do, we shall see that this is not nearly the number that is being mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: So, in conclusion - and I'm now referring to paragraph number 28 in the fifth amended indictment - it reads as follows: "Prior to the 17th of April, 1992, almost 17.000 Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims of a total population of 33.000 lived in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Following the forcible takeover of the Bosanski Samac municipality by Serb forces, the majority of the non-Serb residents fled or were forced," and so on and so. These are the figures that are mentioned, and you are challenging these figures. Do I understand you correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not challenging; I'm simply telling you facts. You can't say that Prud was expelled anywhere, because it was not in the Serbian municipality of Samac, so it couldn't be expelled. Domaljevac, Bazik, Grebnice, were not in the Serbian municipality of Samac. You cannot speak of the expulsion of the people from Kornica when they were not part of the Serbian municipality of Samac. The same goes for Srednja Slatina. None of these places were in the area. I wish I had a map here so that I could show you what this looks like. It's hard now to tell you these numbers off the top of my head, but Domaljevac had over 6.000 inhabitants, and these people were never expelled. They remained there. Bazik had 2.000 and they remained there. Grebnice, almost all of them remained in Grebnice. Prud, almost everyone remained in Prud. Kornica, everybody remained in Kornica. Part of Slatina, Srednja Slatina or central Slatina, everybody stayed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions. I think Mr. Tadic has now given us a very clear demographic picture, which I hope will be corroborated by an expert witness later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, we are about to run out of tape. I've just been informed. So if there is anything you want to add, maybe we should have a break. We can have a 20-minute break and then come back. We'll take our break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to say two or three sentences about these interpretations relating to the taking of bribes. I didn't want to spoil the Prosecutor's line of questioning, and I want to say this for the sake of my descendents, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tadic. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In here is a photograph of my grandchildren. I swear that everything that has been said about money is a fabrication. I never asked anyone to give me money, nor have I ever taken money from anyone. I include Serbs, together with Muslims and Croats, because many Serbs have said the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do you wish it to be reflected in the record that the witness held a Bible in his hand while he said those words? Just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't say that these were the holy scriptures, and inside is a photo of my grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This is on order. Thank you, Mr. Tadic. We have now finished with your evidence and you may return to your usual seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the other witnesses are the videolink and the Rule 92 bis; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The Defence of Mr. Miroslav Tadic has two more witnesses by videolink. That's next week. And after that, depending on the decision handed down by the Chamber, if there is cross-examination by the OTP, then these witnesses will be called. We have a few more documents to be tendered, and we will consider with the OTP this matter in connection with the lists for exchange, and also another document that is part of the Defence of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Demographic expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is under way. Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence of Mr. Zaric, which is to begin, before we call the first witness into the courtroom, I wish to address the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and ask the Chamber to instruct me, and possibly allow me to put forward a plan for the presentation of evidence on behalf of Mr. Zaric. First I wish to inform you that Mr. Zaric's Defence has received from this Chamber approval to call 18 viva voce witnesses. In view of the number of viva voce witnesses - this is a considerable number and will take some time - we now kindly request that after we complete the examination of these viva voce witnesses, that the Defence of Mr. Zaric pause in its presentation of evidence and then present 92 bis evidence, after which Mr. Zaric would testify. It would be very exhausting for the Defence to have Mr. Zaric testify directly after these 18 witnesses before the Trial Chamber, and this is his decision. I therefore kindly request that you give me instructions as to whether it is possible to organise Mr. Zaric's defence in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just add to this submission of my learned friend. I just received the instruction of my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic, and the position of Defence of Mr. Blagoje Simic is that we would like to oppose this suggestion of my learned friend, since it is not in the interests of Mr. Blagoje Simic. I don't know what is the position of Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why? What are the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because we shall have a certain number of witnesses, each of three Defence teams, and during the testimony of these witnesses, we could have the facts of the importance for this trial proceedings. So we would not like to have Mr. Simo Zaric, at the very end of the case, at the last -- I would say last witness, then we shall not be -- of course we shall have possibility in rebuttal or rejoinder proceedings to clarify some things, but -- simply this is the position of the Defence of Blagoje Simic. I leave it to the Trial Chamber for the final decision, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will allow the Defence of Mr. Simo Zaric to arrange the call of their evidence, including the accused, according to their own strategy. Indeed, every accused person is free to arrange their own presentation of the defence, according to their own strategy. The Trial Chamber hasn't given any instructions contrary to that, so I don't see why Mr. Pantelic should have any objection. He decided how he was going to present the defence of his own client, according to his own strategy. The only thing is: Because of the complications we have -- for instance, we have videolink witnesses coming more or less in the middle, we have to deal with that because of the mechanics of arranging for a videolink. So there we have no choice. We have to hear all the witnesses at the same time, regardless of whose defence they are supporting. Otherwise, for the rest of the arrangements, it depends on the Defence counsel, together with the instructions of his own client. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just add, in order to clarify the position: If that would be the case, we don't have any objections to the position of Mr. Zaric's Defence to have all their witnesses and finally including the accused, Mr. Zaric, by the end of their case. But accordingly, we would like to have our 92 bis witnesses after the closing of Mr. Zaric's case. Simple as that. According to our strategy. So if it's not in big contrast with the other Defence teams, that would be the position of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think there is a misunderstanding here. Because the Trial Chamber is aware that you still have your Rule the 92 bis witnesses to call. My earlier ruling does not mean that your witnesses can't come before Mr. Zaric's defence is concluded. I'm just discussing Mr. Zaric's defence, the sequence of calling their evidence. Whether some witnesses will come and then another person's witnesses will come in the middle and -- you know, that's what I was discussing. That's what I was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with that at all. But the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the Trial Chamber is looking at the statements to decide which ones should come for cross-examination. So the ruling will be given in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we'll proceed and call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Simeunovic. Before we begin, I will give you some instructions in order for your testimony to fulfil its function, or rather, in order that everything you say will be properly recorded. Therefore, if you have any problems in hearing the question, if there is something wrong with the headset, for example, please let me know immediately. Furthermore, I ask you to listen to the question and then pause a few seconds before giving your reply. Don't hurry too much, but don't speak too slowly either. You will find the pace that will enable the interpreters to hear you, and then the Chamber will be able to follow through the interpretation your testimony. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you, and I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Maksim Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of August, 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: My place of birth is Pelagicevo, in the municipality of Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what country Pelagicevo, the town and the municipality, is?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you live up to the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the 17th of April, 1992, I lived in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Where do you live now? In what town?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I still live in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children have you got?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I have one child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell me what school you completed?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I have five levels of education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell us what your status is now, what you do now?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army? When and where?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did serve in the Yugoslav People's Army, in the school for reserve officers of armoured and mechanised units. I went to school in Banja Luka and I did my training period in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where Osijek is after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What rank did you have as a reserve officer when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I left the JNA as a lieutenant colonel of armoured mechanised units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me from when to when?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member from 1967 until the League of Communists of Yugoslavia ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After the League of Communists of Yugoslavia ceased to exist, did you become a member of another political party?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I became a member of the SDP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that short for the Social Democrats?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that party in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a party which sort of continued the work of the Communists' League of Yugoslavia, in a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you now presently a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am a member of the league -- my apologies. I am a member of the Socialist Party of the -- of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us: What is your ethnic background, your nationality?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which religion do you belong to?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Christian, an Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you completed your compulsory military service with the JNA, what was your military assignment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of my military service, and pursuant to an order of the Ministry for All People's Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, my assignment was to a war unit of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's get this clear straight away. These were not Territorial Defence units of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't Territorial Defence units of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were assigned to this military unit, what was your position within that unit?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the 2nd Armoured Battalion of the 395th Brigade in Brcko. I was the assistant commander for information and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which year that happened?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was in March 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how long you stayed with that war assignment and in that position?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I kept this assignment and my position as the assistant commander for information and security -- I stayed until the 8th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned from your military service in the JNA, where did you find a job?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of my military service, I found a job in the Luka company based in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay with that company, and did you change jobs; if so, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I worked for six years for the Luka company in Brcko, and then I changed jobs and I went to work with the JNA as civilian staff. I was a mechanic in charge of weapon maintenance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: What does civilian staff working for the JNA really mean?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian staff, or a civilian working for a JNA, is usually a person charged with certain tasks. The working hours start at 8.00 in the morning. And these persons never wear uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do such persons have any military authority?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, we had no military authority, in the sense of power to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a particularly favourable conditions for retirement?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. We had the same conditions for retirement as all other citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who worked in other sectors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us now: From that job, from that position as civilian staff in the JNA, where did you go, and when did that stop?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I stopped working as civilian staff in the JNA when I responded to the mobilisation call-up and when I reported to my war unit of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you specify when exactly this happened, which unit that was, and which position within that unit you assumed?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was the 2nd Armoured Battalion of the 395th Motorised Brigade with headquarters in Brcko. I responded to the mobilisation call-up in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of this unit?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 2nd Armoured Battalion was in the village of Donji Zabar, Orasje municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there in Donji Zabar, Orasje municipality --

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived there. We reached the command post in mid-October. I can't remember the exact date, but it was in mid-October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, in that territory, in that area, did any military formation of the JNA exist which you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, and we were within their zone of responsibility and we were immediately subordinated to that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know pursuant to whose order the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA was set up?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know pursuant to whose order. The 17th Tactical Group was set up pursuant to the commander General Savo Jankovic's order, who was the commander of the 17th Corps, based in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which area was covered by the zone of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group were covered part of Brcko municipality, Orasje municipality, Bosanski Samac municipality, and part of Gradacac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which military formations did the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA comprise?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th Tactical Group of the JNA comprised the command of the 17th Tactical Group, communications company, military police, five infantry squads of the JNA, and the armoured battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This armoured battalion is the battalion in which you were working as the officer in charge of information and security?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the battalion which was first in the 395th Brigade and then became part of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please just tell us: Who was the commander of that armoured battalion?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Major Dusko Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order on the setting up of the 17th Tactical Group, General Savo Jankovic also appointed Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic as the commander of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the chief in the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the 17th Tactical Group, pursuant to the same order, was Major Brajkovic. I can't remember his last name -- I mean his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Commander Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic and Chief Brajkovic originally hailed from, from which republic of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did they hail from?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I know they were both born in the Republic of Serbia, but their places of birth specifically, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only wanted to know about the Republic, nothing else. Can you please tell us when you became the assistant commander for information and security in the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order by the commander of the 17th Corps of the JNA, General Savo Jankovic, I was moved from the armoured battalion, where I was assistant commander for information and security, and became part of the 17th Tactical Group. I became chief for information and security on the 8th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether detachments from the 17th Tactical Group had assistant commanders for intelligence and information?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each detachment had an assistant commander. There was the commander, the assistant commander, the deputy commander, and the assistant for intelligence and security, and this also applies to the armoured battalion from which I came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 4th Detachment of the JNA, which was part of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that. The assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 4th Detachment of the JNA, with headquarters in the town of Samac, that was Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the 4th Detachment of the JNA was?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. The commander was Radovan Antic, a captain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the purview of your duties, did you ever go to the command of the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go, quite often. I went to all the commands, because that was part of my duty. I did rounds visiting the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then please tell us: Where was the command of the 4th Detachment of the JNA located precisely?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 4th Detachment of the JNA was located in Sit, the Samac textile industry in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whenever you were there, did you see any symbols on those buildings, or any other marks?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On the building where the command of the 4th Detachment was based, there was the Yugoslav flag, and next to it there was the flag of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the detachment was structured, how it was organised? Was it life in the barracks or was it a different kind of thing? Can you tell us about the way the 4th Detachment looked and functioned, and then about the other detachments which were part of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment, as well as all the other detachments which were part of the 17th Tactical Group, they didn't have any barracks at their disposal. We say the command of the detachment. Those were actually two simple offices, offices which were part of the factory. Those were being used by the command of the detachment, but there were no barracks to speak of. That was just the formal headquarters of the command. And there was a duty roster for members of the command who worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: How was it with the members of the detachment? What were their activities? How was their life organised?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC
utterances.text: The other members, that's soldiers in detachments, as I said, they had no barracks. They were just registered as members of the 4th Detachment. They had their duties. They were given specific tasks, but they stayed at their own homes and they went about their tasks in the local economy agricultural tasks or perhaps their own private activities and businesses. But they lived and slept at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I think this may be a convenient moment to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of February 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
